docs.title: Welcome to ROXAS AI
docs.text:
ROXAS AI is an open-source, Python-based tool designed to streamline quantitative wood anatomy (QWA) research. By integrating state-of-the-art AI analysis methods into the napari platform, it enables researchers to efficiently establish long, high-resolution time series of cell measurements within dated tree rings.

Currently optimized for linear conifer anatomies, ROXAS AI provides an end-to-end workflow—from automated image segmentation to visual cross-dating—allowing for precise dendroecological and wood anatomical studies on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

docs.title: Why ROXAS AI?
docs.text:
ROXAS AI was developed to modernize and expand upon the foundations of the classical ROXAS implementation. It directly addresses several long-standing limitations to make wood anatomy more accessible and scalable:

  • Cross-Platform Accessibility: Unlike the classical version, which is restricted to Windows, ROXAS AI runs natively on all major operating systems.
  • Open Research & Powerful Viewing: It removes the dependency on expensive third-party software (like Image-Pro Plus). Instead, by using the open-source image viewer napari, ROXAS AI leverages a powerful workhorse for image viewing with an intuitive and versatile editing toolbox.
  • Modern AI Segmentation: By leveraging specialized deep-learning neural networks (Katzenmaier et al. 2023, 2025), it overcomes the limitations of classical image segmentation, handling complex wood structures with higher accuracy and less manual intervention (see Segmentation Models).
  • Ease of Use: It reduces the requirement for expert-level configuration knowledge, making professional-grade wood anatomical analysis more intuitive.

docs.title: Installation & Setup Guide
docs.text: Welcome to ROXAS AI! This guide walks you through setting up a clean Python environment, installing the napari-roxas-ai plugin, and configuring optional GPU acceleration for fast deep-learning inference.

docs.title: Step 1: Install a Package Manager & Open Terminal
docs.text:
We strongly recommend installing Miniforge (recommended for scientific computing with conda-forge defaults) or Miniconda to manage your Python environment.

WindowsmacOSLinux
  1. Download the installer:
    • Miniforge (Recommended): Download the Miniforge Windows 64-bit Installer.
    • Miniconda (Alternative): Download the Miniconda Windows 64-bit Installer.
  2. Run the installer: Follow the standard setup wizard.
  3. Open the prompt:
    • Open the Windows Start menu and search for Miniforge Prompt (or Anaconda Prompt if using Miniconda).
    • Open it to run the subsequent commands.
  1. Download the installer:
    • Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4): Download Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.pkg or the Miniconda Apple Silicon Installer.
    • Intel Macs: Download Miniforge3-MacOSX-x86_64.pkg or the Miniconda Intel Installer.
  2. Run the installer package and follow the prompts.
  3. Alternative (Command-line installation via Terminal): 
    curl -L -O "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-MacOSX-$(uname -m).sh"
bash Miniforge3-MacOSX-$(uname -m).sh
  4. Open Terminal: Open Applications > Utilities > Terminal.
  1. Download the installer in Terminal:
    • x86_64 (64-bit Intel/AMD): 
      wget https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
bash Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
    • ARM64 / aarch64: 
      wget https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-aarch64.sh
bash Miniforge3-Linux-aarch64.sh
  2. Follow the installer prompts and allow it to initialize Conda for your shell.
  3. Open a new Terminal window afterwards.

docs.title: Step 2: Create & Activate the Environment
docs.text:
Create a clean Python 3.12 environment named roxas-ai and activate it:

conda create -n roxas-ai python=3.12
conda activate roxas-ai

Always activate your environment

Whenever you open a new terminal session to run ROXAS AI, make sure to activate the environment first using conda activate roxas-ai.

docs.title: Step 3: (Optional) GPU Acceleration
docs.text:
While ROXAS AI functions fully on CPU, enabling GPU acceleration significantly speeds up deep-learning segmentation on large high-resolution images.

Windows & Linux (NVIDIA GPUs)macOS (Apple Silicon & Intel)

By default, PyPI installs a CPU-only build of PyTorch on Windows and Linux. To leverage your NVIDIA GPU:

  1. Install CUDA-enabled PyTorch: 

    pip install torch torchvision \
  --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
    This single command supports all recent NVIDIA GPUs (RTX 20-series, 30-series, 40-series, and 50-series / Blackwell). The CUDA runtime is bundled with the wheels, so no separate CUDA toolkit installation is needed—only an up-to-date NVIDIA display driver.

    (Note: If your system uses an older display driver that cannot be updated, you can install the CUDA 12.6 build instead by replacing cu128 with cu126).

  2. Verify GPU / CUDA availability: 

    python -c "
import torch
print('CUDA available:', torch.cuda.is_available())
print('CUDA version:', torch.version.cuda)
print('GPU:', torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'None')
"
    For a functional GPU installation, CUDA available: should output True and list your GPU device name.

  3. Troubleshooting: If CUDA available: reports False after installation (e.g., if a CPU-only PyTorch build was previously cached or installed), cleanly remove PyTorch and reinstall: 

    pip uninstall torch torchvision torchaudio -y
pip install torch torchvision \
  --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

(For supported AMD GPUs on Linux, consult the PyTorch ROCm installation guide).

  • Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4): PyTorch leverages Apple's Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) backend natively. No separate CUDA or driver installation is necessary. The standard ROXAS AI package includes the appropriate PyTorch build.

To verify MPS availability on Apple Silicon: 

python -c "
import torch
print('MPS available:', torch.backends.mps.is_available())
print('MPS built:', torch.backends.mps.is_built())
"
When MPS available: True is displayed, ROXAS AI will accelerate cell segmentation using your Apple GPU.

  • Intel-based Macs: GPU acceleration is not supported on Intel Macs; ROXAS AI will run automatically using the CPU.

docs.title: Step 4: Install ROXAS AI
docs.text:
Install the latest released version of napari-roxas-ai via pip:

pip install napari-roxas-ai

docs.title: Step 5: Launch & Verify
docs.text:
1. Launch napari: 
    napari
  2. Open sample data:
  3. In the napari menu, navigate to File > Open Sample > ROXAS AI.
  4. Three layers (Image, Rings, and Cells) will load into the viewer.

Automatic Background Model Downloads

Pre-trained neural network weights (.pth / .pt files) and sample data are automatically downloaded in the background when first accessed and cached locally for all future sessions. Download progress is logged in your terminal window.

  1. Enable GPU acceleration in Settings (if applicable):
  2. In napari, go to Plugins > ROXAS AI > ZZ - Settings.
  3. Expand the processing section.
  4. Check the boxes for try_to_use_gpu and try_to_use_autocast.
  5. Click Apply.
  6. The settings take effect immediately (no restart required), though any segmentation or measurement run already in progress will complete with the settings it was started with.

docs.title: Summary Checklist
docs.text:
• [x] Miniforge / Miniconda installed and opened in the terminal.
  • [x] Dedicated Python 3.12 environment created and activated (conda activate roxas-ai).
  • [x] (Optional) GPU PyTorch installed and tested (CUDA available: True / MPS available: True).
  • [x] napari-roxas-ai installed via pip.
  • [x] napari launched and sample data loaded successfully.
  • [x] (Optional) try_to_use_gpu enabled in ZZ - Settings.

Important note

Do not install packages into the environment while napari or another Python process is actively running in it. Always perform package installations and updates from a dedicated terminal prompt before launching napari.

docs.title: Deep-Learning Segmentation Models
docs.text: Technical details about the deep-learning neural network architectures, inference pipelines, and scientific literature behind automated segmentation in ROXAS AI.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ROXAS AI replaces classical threshold- and edge-based image processing with deep learning models trained specifically on wood anatomical micro-sections and surface scans. This enables robust, automated detection of both individual tracheid cell lumina and annual tree-ring boundaries across challenging image conditions (e.g., uneven staining, compression wood, or anatomical distortions).

Models run locally on your machine using PyTorch and PyTorch Lightning, with automatic hardware acceleration when a compatible GPU (CUDA or Apple Silicon MPS) is detected.

docs.title: Cell Segmentation Model
docs.text: The cell segmentation model automatically detects and delineates individual tracheid cell lumina in high-resolution conifer cross-sections.

docs.title: Architecture & Pipeline
docs.text:
• Network Architecture: A U-Net semantic segmentation architecture equipped with a ResNet-50 encoder backbone (via segmentation_models_pytorch).
  • Tiled Patch Inference: High-resolution scans (which often span tens of thousands of pixels) are processed in overlapping tiles (\(1024 \times 1024\text{ px}\) with an \(800\text{ px}\) stride).
  • Reflection Padding: To eliminate boundary and edge distortions at patch margins, inputs are padded in reflect mode (\(112\text{ px}\) margin), and only the unpadded central regions are stitched back into the final sample mask.
  • Instance Labeling: The binary lumen predictions are transformed into unique Cell IDs (CID) via connected-component labeling (skimage.measure.label).

docs.title: Tree-Ring Boundary Segmentation Model
docs.text: The tree-ring boundary model identifies annual ring boundaries in wood samples, defining annual growth increments for dendrochronological analysis.

docs.title: Methodology & Formulation
docs.text:
• Iterative Boundary Regression: Rather than performing standard pixel-wise segmentation, the model detects ring boundary trajectories sequentially along the radial growth axis, formulating boundary line identification as an iterative regression problem.
  • Post-Processing & Ordering: Identified boundary trajectories are sorted continuously from bark to pith, extended across the sample width, and converted into labeled annual ring bands.
  • Relation to Published Model: The ring boundary model implemented in ROXAS AI is based on the deep-learning regression framework introduced in Katzenmaier et al. (2025). Note that while the published paper demonstrates the approach for angiosperms and circular sample geometries, the model integrated in this version of the app is adapted for linear conifer anatomies.

docs.title: Model Weights & Automatic Management
docs.text:
• Default Checkpoints: Pre-trained weights for the cell model (linear_cells_model.pth) and ring model (LinearRingModel_v3_iterative.pt / linear_rings_model.pth) are managed automatically.
  • Automatic Downloads: If model weights are not found in the local installation directory, ROXAS AI automatically downloads them in the background from remote asset storage upon first use.
  • Caching: Once downloaded, model checkpoints are cached locally and reused for all subsequent single-image and batch-processing runs.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Katzenmaier et al. 2023: Katzenmaier, M., Sainte Fare Garnot, V., Björklund, J., Schneider, L., Wegner, J. D., & von Arx, G. (2023). Towards ROXAS AI: deep learning for faster and more accurate conifer cell analysis. Dendrochronologia, 81:126126. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dendro.2023.126126
  • Katzenmaier et al. 2025: Katzenmaier, M., Garnot, V. S. F., Wegner, J. D., & von Arx, G. (2025). Towards ROXAS AI: automatic multi-species ring boundaries segmentation as regression in anatomical images. Frontiers in Plant Science, 16:1516635. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2025.1516635

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Technical details about the files created by ROXAS AI and the numeric output variables.

docs.title: Image Orientation Requirements
docs.text: Linear input images have to be oriented with +/- horizontal rings and the bark side at the bottom.

docs.title: File Formats
docs.text: ROXAS AI uses a standardized naming convention to organize analysis data. For a sample named sample_01, the following files are typically generated:

docs.title: Spatial & Image Files
docs.text:
• .scan.jpg / .scan.tif etc.: The original high-resolution scan of the wood sample; supported image formats: JPG, JPEG, TIFF, TIF, PNG, BMP, JP2.
  • .cells.png: A label image produced by the deep-learning cell segmentation model (Segmentation Models) where each pixel value corresponds to a unique cell ID (CID).
  • .rings.tif: A label image (or vector-like representation) produced by the deep-learning ring boundary segmentation model (Segmentation Models) containing the identified tree-ring boundaries.
  • _annotated.jpg: A visualization of the scan with ring boundaries and year labels overlaid for quick review. This file is automatically generated and saved whenever the .rings layer is saved.
  • .ReferenceSeries.jpg: (Optional) A visual representation of the reference chronologies used during cross-dating.

docs.title: Data & Metadata Files
docs.text:
• .metadata.json: A comprehensive JSON file containing sample information, imaging parameters, and all processing thresholds required to reproduce the analysis.
  • .cells_table.csv: A CSV file (semicolon-delimited by default, configurable in settings) containing measurements for every individual cell.
  • .rings_table.csv: A CSV file (semicolon-delimited by default, configurable in settings) containing aggregated measurements for each tree ring.

docs.title: Output Variables (Acronyms)
docs.text: The output tables (.cells_table.csv and .rings_table.csv) use standardized acronyms. Most measurements are provided in micrometers (\(\mu\text{m}\)) or square micrometers (\(\mu\text{m}^2\)).

docs.title: Missing Values & Error Codes
docs.text: Missing values or empty fields are left blank (NA) in the CSV output to ensure compatibility with modern data analysis tools like R and Python.

docs.title: Theoretical Hydraulic Conductance (KH)
docs.text:
The theoretical hydraulic conductance is approximated by Poiseuille's law and adjusted for elliptical tubes (Nonweiler 1975):

\[ \text{KH} = \frac{\text{LA} \cdot m^2}{\nu \cdot k} \]

Where: - LA: Lumen area (\(\text{m}^2\)) - \(\nu\): Viscosity of water (\(1.002 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\text{Pa}\cdot\text{s}\) at 20°C) - \(m\): Mean hydraulic radius (\(\pi ab / C\)) - \(k\): Geometry coefficient (\(4 / (1 + \sqrt{1 - e^4})\)) - \(e\): Eccentricity of the ellipse

docs.title: Mork's Index (Radial Thickness-to-Span Ratio, RTSR, Figure 1)
docs.text:
Mork's index distinguishes earlywood from latewood tracheids based on the ratio between tangential cell wall thickness and radial lumen diameter (Denne 1989):

Figure 1: Definition of Mork's index based on tangential cell wall thickness and radial lumen diameter.

A tracheid is classified as latewood when the ratio between twice the double tangential cell wall thickness (4x CWTTAN) and its radial lumen width (DRAD) is larger than 1.

docs.title: Cell Wall Reinforcement Index (TB2, Figure 2)
docs.text:
The cell wall reinforcement index estimates conduit resistance against cell wall collapse under negative hydraulic pressure (Hacke et al. 2001):

Figure 2: Definition of the cell wall reinforcement index \((t/b)^2\).

The index is calculated as \((t/b)^2\), where \(t\) is the thickness of the shared double cell wall and \(b\) is the internal lumen diameter span across the corresponding orientation, taking the minimum of radial and tangential ratios.

docs.title: Cell Wall Thickness (CWT) Quality Control & Filtering
docs.text: To obtain robust, artifact-free anatomical measurements, ROXAS AI applies automated multi-stage quality control filters to all raw cell wall thickness measurements.

docs.title: 1. Wall Definitions & Measurement Integration (Figure 3)
docs.text: Figure 3: Definition of tangential and radial wall orientations and the central measurement integration span.

docs.title: Cell Wall Identification Algorithm
docs.text:
To measure the cell wall thickness of individual cells from segmented lumen masks, ROXAS AI uses an automated Euclidean distance and watershed-based approach:

  1. Lumen Boundaries & Euclidean Distance Mask: Based on the segmented cell lumina, an inverted binary mask is created where background and cell walls are foreground pixels. A Euclidean distance transform is calculated across this mask, computing the exact spatial distance of every wall pixel to the nearest cell lumen boundary.
  2. Watershed Mask & Middle Lamella Approximation: A watershed segmentation algorithm is computed between adjacent cell lumina to detect the contact boundary (the watershed line) between neighboring tracheids. Following Prendin et al. (2017), the exact position of the middle lamella separating two adjacent cells cannot be resolved directly from optical lumen contours alone; it is therefore geometrically approximated by assuming that each wall of two adjacent sharing cells has equal thickness (i.e., the middle lamella is located equidistant between the two lumina along the watershed ridge).
  3. Lateral Integration: For each of the four anatomical wall sectors (CWTPI, CWTBA, CWTLE, CWTRI), distance values are sampled along the watershed line. To avoid geometric distortion at rounded cell corners, measurements are laterally integrated over the central portion of the wall (defined by relwidth_cwt_integration, default: 75%).

docs.title: Wall Sectors & Aggregated Metrics
docs.text:
For each conifer tracheid, cell walls are measured across four distinct anatomical orientations:

  • Tangential walls: CWTPI (pith-facing, top) and CWTBA (bark-facing, bottom).
  • Radial walls: CWTLE (left) and CWTRI (right).
  • Integration span: Wall thicknesses are integrated over the central span of each wall segment (defined by relwidth_cwt_integration, default: 75%) to avoid corner-rounding biases.
  • Aggregated metrics:
    • Tangential mean: CWTTAN = (CWTPI + CWTBA) / 2; or any of the two if the other NA
    • Radial mean: CWTRAD = (CWTLE + CWTRI) / 2; or any of the two if the other NA
    • Overall mean: CWTALL = (CWTTAN + CWTRAD) / 2; or any of the two if the other NA

docs.title: 2. Global IQR Distribution Filter / Tukey's Fences (Figure 4)
docs.text:
Figure 4: Global IQR outlier filtering based on lower and upper Tukey's fences.

To exclude segmentation debris, extreme clumps, or sub-pixel erosion artifacts, measurements are filtered against population-wide distributions computed independently for tangential walls (CWTPI, CWTBA) and radial walls (CWTLE, CWTRI), based on the Interquartile Range (\(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\)):

  • Lower Limit: \(\max(Q_1 - 1.5 \cdot \text{IQR},\, 1\text{ pixel in }\mu\text{m})\) (controlled by lower_limit_cwt_iqr_multiplier)
  • Upper Limit: \(Q_3 + 3.0 \cdot \text{IQR}\) (controlled by upper_limit_cwt_iqr_multiplier)
  • Values falling outside Lower Limit: or Upper Limit: are set to blank (NA).

docs.title: 3. Opposite Wall Ratio Filter (Figure 5)
docs.text:
Figure 5: Opposite wall ratio filter identifying and removing inflated wall measurements bordering ray cells.

In conifer xylem, opposing walls of a single tracheid have comparable thicknesses unless bordering a different cell type (such as wood ray cells) or an intercellular gap.

  • Rule: If the thickness of one wall exceeds opposite_cwt_ratio_limit \(\cdot\) opposing wall thickness (default threshold: 1.5), the inflated side is excluded (NA), while the valid opposing side is retained.
  • Anatomical and technical context: Because the distance-to-watershed algorithm assumes equal double-wall thickness between adjacent detected lumina (Prendin et al. 2017), unsegmented or narrower intervening structures like uniseriate wood ray parenchyma cells are not recognized as independent tracheid lumina. Consequently, the Euclidean distance measured across the entire ray gap between two tracheid files is assigned as a single inflated tracheid wall (CWTRI in Figure 5). The filter identifies this asymmetric inflation relative to the normal opposing wall (CWTLE), discarding the artifactual CWTRI measurement while preserving CWTLE.

docs.title: 4. Adjacent Wall Ratio Filter (Figure 6)
docs.text:
Figure 6: Adjacent wall ratio filter detecting and discarding local segmentation anomalies.

Protects against severe local segmentation anomalies (e.g., pit aperture artifacts, small pollutions, tracheids sandwiched between two rays) that disproportionately distort a single wall relative to the tracheid's perpendicular dimensions.

  • Rule: If an individual tangential wall thickness exceeds adjacent_cwt_ratio_limit (default threshold: 3.0), the distorted tangential wall is set to NA (and vice versa for radial walls!).

docs.title: The Metadata File (.metadata.json)
docs.text: The metadata file ensures traceability and reproducibility of your analysis. It stores four main categories of information:

docs.title: 1. Sample & Project Information
docs.text:
• sample_name: The unique identifier for the wood sample.
  • sample_stem_path: The relative path of the sample within the project directory.
  • sample_type: The type of wood (i.e., conifer or angiosperm; note that the angiosperm analysis is not implemented yet).
  • meas_geometry: The measurement layout (i.e., linear or circular; note that the circular analysis is not implemented yet).
  • rings_outmost_complete_year: The calendar year assigned to the most recent complete tree ring.
  • reference_series: The cross-dating reference series used (or NA if none).

docs.title: 2. Imaging & Spatial Metadata
docs.text:
• spatial_resolution: The conversion factor from pixels to micrometers (\(\text{px}/\mu\text{m}\)). This is critical for all subsequent physical measurements.
  • scan_size: The dimensions of the original image in pixels (Height, Width).
  • scan_info: Detailed technical info about the image, including the detected DPI (Dots Per Inch).
  • scan_exif: Metadata extracted directly from the image file (e.g., software used for scanning, capture date).

docs.title: 3. Processing & Traceability
docs.text:
• sw_version: The exact version of ROXAS AI used for the analysis.
  • meas_by: The username or system identifier that ran the measurement analysis.
  • cells_segmentation_model & rings_segmentation_model: The specific AI model filenames (.pth / .pt) used for detection.
  • meas_created_at: A timestamp of when the final measurement table was generated.

docs.title: 4. Analysis Parameters & Quality Control
docs.text:
These parameters define how cell walls are measured and how clusters are handled:

  • cluster_dbl_cwt_threshold: Threshold for detecting cell wall clusters (physiological grouping via pits). Used for angiosperms.
  • relwidth_cwt_integration: The relative width along the cell wall used for integrating thickness measurements.
  • lower_limit_cwt_iqr_multiplier: Multiplier for the lower Tukey's fence (\(Q_1 - k \cdot \text{IQR}\)) in cell wall thickness outlier detection.
  • upper_limit_cwt_iqr_multiplier: Multiplier for the upper Tukey's fence (\(Q_3 + k \cdot \text{IQR}\)) in cell wall thickness outlier detection.
  • opposite_cwt_ratio_limit: Quality control factor comparing wall thickness on opposite sides of a cell.
  • adjacent_cwt_ratio_limit: Quality control factor comparing wall thickness on adjacent sides of a cell.

docs.title: Global Settings (settings.json)
docs.text:
While the .metadata.json is unique to each sample, the settings.json file stores your global preferences and plugin configurations.

Important: One of the core goals of ROXAS AI is to be accessible. Unlike classical systems, no expert knowledge is required to configure these settings. For most users, the default values are optimized for professional results and do not need to be changed.

The settings are organized into several logical blocks:

docs.title: 1. File Extensions (file_extensions)
docs.text:
Defines how ROXAS AI recognizes and names files:

  • scan_file_extension: [".scan", ".jpg"]
  • cells_file_extension: [".cells", ".png"]
  • cells_table_file_extension: [".cells_table", ".csv"]
  • rings_file_extension: [".rings", ".tif"]
  • rings_table_file_extension: [".rings_table", ".csv"]
  • metadata_file_extension: [".metadata", ".json"]
  • crossdating_file_extension: [".crossdating", ".txt"]
  • roxas_file_extensions: List of managed ROXAS file suffixes ([".scan", ".cells", ".rings", ".metadata"]).
  • image_file_extensions: Supported image formats ([".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".tif", ".tiff", ".bmp", ".jp2"]).
  • text_file_extensions: Supported text and table formats ([".rwl", ".tuc", ".txt", ".csv", ".tsv"]).

docs.title: 2. Processing & GPU (processing)
docs.text:
Allows configuring hardware acceleration and memory optimization:

  • try_to_use_gpu: Set to true to enable GPU acceleration if a compatible CUDA-enabled graphics card is available.
  • try_to_use_autocast: Set to true for mixed precision acceleration during deep learning inference.

docs.title: 3. Tables (tables)
docs.text:
Defines the output format for tabular data:

  • separator: Column delimiter for output tables (default: ";").
  • index_column: Column identifier name (default: "id").

docs.title: 4. Visualization (Vectorization & Rasterization)
docs.text:
Controls how data appears in the napari viewer:

  • vectorization: Controls polygon smoothing tolerances, edge widths, and colors for cells (cells_edge_width, cells_edge_color, cells_face_color, cells_tolerance) and rings (rings_edge_width, rings_edge_color, rings_tolerance, rerun_interactive_edge_color).
  • rasterization: Controls color sequences for adjacent rings (rings_color_sequence), uncomplete rings (uncomplete_ring_value, uncomplete_ring_color), and cell masks (cells_color).

docs.title: 5. Measurement Defaults (measurements)
docs.text:
Contains default parameters for anatomical analysis, used to populate metadata for new samples:

  • cluster_dbl_cwt_threshold: Threshold for detecting cell wall clusters (physiological grouping via pits). Used for angiosperms.
  • cells_smoothing_kernel_size: Size of the kernel used for smoothing cell boundaries.
  • relwidth_cwt_integration: The relative width along the cell wall used for thickness calculations.
  • cells_tangential_angle: Default angle for tangential orientation.
  • lower_limit_cwt_iqr_multiplier: Multiplier for the lower Tukey's fence (\(Q_1 - k \cdot \text{IQR}\)) in cell wall thickness outlier detection.
  • upper_limit_cwt_iqr_multiplier: Multiplier for the upper Tukey's fence (\(Q_3 + k \cdot \text{IQR}\)) in cell wall thickness outlier detection.
  • opposite_cwt_ratio_limit: Quality control factor comparing wall thickness on opposite sides of a cell.
  • adjacent_cwt_ratio_limit: Quality control factor comparing wall thickness on adjacent sides of a cell.

docs.title: 6. Image Compression & Project Directory
docs.text:
• JPEG_compression: Quality, optimization, and progressive encoding settings for saved JPEG images (e.g., annotated rings overlay).
  • project_directory: Path to the currently active project working directory.

docs.title: 7. Metadata Field Definitions (samples_metadata)
docs.text:
Defines the structure, validation rules, and widget types for the input forms in the plugin:

  • sample_name: Text input for the unique sample identifier.
  • sample_type: Dropdown selection for wood type (conifer, angiosperm).
  • meas_geometry: Dropdown selection for measurement layout (linear, circular).
  • spatial_resolution: Numeric input for spatial resolution in \(\text{px}/\mu\text{m}\).
  • rings_outmost_complete_year: Integer input for the calendar year of the outermost complete ring.

docs.title: Tutorials & Workflows
docs.text: Step-by-step guides for quantitative wood anatomy (QWA) and dendrochronological analysis using ROXAS AI in napari.

docs.title: 1. Quickstart: 5-Minute Single Sample Walkthrough
docs.text:
This fast-track walkthrough gets you from raw image to measured anatomical traits using the bundled conifer sample.

flowchart LR
    A["Load Conifer Sample"] --> B["Detect Cells & Rings (3A)"]
    B --> C["Review Annotations (5 & 6)"]
    C --> D["Measure Traits (9A)"]

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Built-in Sample Data
docs.text:
1. Launch napari.
  2. Navigate to the top menu: File > Open Sample > ROXAS AI > Conifer Sample Data.
  3. ROXAS AI automatically loads the conifer cross-section scan along with pre-configured spatial metadata (\(\mu\text{m}/\text{px}\)).

Figure 1: Conifer sample dataset loaded into the napari viewer.

docs.title: Step 2: Run Deep Learning Detection
docs.text:
1. Open the plugin menu: Plugins > ROXAS AI > 3A - Detect cells & rings (individual image).
  2. Ensure the active image is selected in the Sample Image dropdown.
  3. Select the segmentation models:
  4. Cells Model: linear_cells_model
  5. Rings Model: linear_rings_model
  6. Click Run Segmentation. Deep-learning inference generates two new layers: .cells (cell lumen labels) and .rings (ring boundary labels).

Figure 2: Automated cell lumen and tree-ring boundary segmentation overlay.

docs.title: Step 3: Quick Visual Verification
docs.text:
1. Toggle layer visibility in the left napari layer list to inspect the overlay against the anatomical scan.
  2. Use Plugins > ROXAS AI > 6 - Edit rings or 5 - Edit cells if minor adjustments are needed.

docs.title: Step 4: Extract Cell & Ring Measurements
docs.text:
1. Open Plugins > ROXAS AI > 9A - Measure cells & rings (individual image).
  2. Select the active sample and click Run Measurements.
  3. Measurement output tables (.cells_table.txt and .rings_table.txt) are created in the project folder with comprehensive anatomical metrics (lumen area, cell wall thickness, Mork's index, ring widths).

Figure 3: Measurement completion with generated tabular files.

docs.title: 2. Standard Workflow: Tree-Ring & Cell Anatomy Time Series
docs.text:
This comprehensive, step-by-step workflow describes the standard protocol for generating publication-quality dendroclimatic and wood anatomical time series from raw microsections or high-resolution surface scans.

flowchart TD
    P1["Step 1: Project Setup & Image Preparation"] --> P2["Step 2: Automated Cell & Ring Detection (3A)"]
    P2 --> P3["Step 3: High-Accuracy Lumen & Cell Wall Editing (5)"]
    P3 --> P4["Step 4: Tree-Ring Boundary Curation (6)"]
    P4 --> P5["Step 5: Visual Cross-Dating (7)"]
    P5 --> P6["Step 6: Save Annotations (8)"]
    P6 --> P7["Step 7: Trait Extraction (9A)"]

docs.title: Step 1: Project Setup & Image Preparation
docs.text:
1. Open Plugins > ROXAS AI > 0 - Define project directory and choose the root directory where your analysis files will reside.
  2. Open Plugins > ROXAS AI > 1 - Prepare project images for analysis.
  3. The preparation assistant scans your folder for raw images (.tif, .jpg, .png, etc.) and opens the Metadata Dialog:
  4. Resolution (\(\mu\text{m}/\text{px}\)): Enter the calibrated micrometer-per-pixel value of your optical microscope or scanner.
  5. Anatomy / Growth Type: Select conifer.
  6. Geometry: Select linear for standard radial increment cores or microsections.
  7. Outermost Ring Year: Set the calendar year of the outermost complete ring (e.g., sampling year 2023).
  8. (Optional) Click Start Processing Crossdating Files to import reference ring-width chronologies (.rwl, .tuc, or tabular .txt/.csv).
  9. Click Prepare Images. The images are standardized to <sample>.scan.<ext> and initialized with <sample>.metadata.json.

Figure 4: Setting spatial resolution and calendar dating parameters in the image preparation dialog.

docs.title: Step 2: Loading & Automated Segmentation
docs.text:
1. Open Plugins > ROXAS AI > 2/4 - Load image(s) and load your prepared sample.
  2. Open Plugins > ROXAS AI > 3A - Detect cells & rings (individual image).
  3. Choose the appropriate neural network models and click Run Segmentation.
  4. Both cell lumen masks and ring boundary contours will populate as interactive napari layers.

Figure 5: Automated cell and ring predictions visualized in napari.

docs.title: Step 3: High-Accuracy Lumen & Cell Wall Editing
docs.text:
Refine cell lumen annotations using Plugins > ROXAS AI > 5 - Edit cells.

Tip: You can save your edits directly from within this widget at any time. Regularly saving edits is a good routine to preserve your work throughout the editing session.

Figure 6: Cell layer editor displaying raster brush/eraser controls and vector polygon conversion.

docs.title: Raster vs. Vector Editing Modes
docs.text:
ROXAS AI offers two complementary editing modes for cell lumina:

Mode Best Used For Tooling & Mechanics Raster Mode Rapid mask cleaning, separating merged cells, filling voids Pixel brush, eraser, paint bucket. Direct modification of the integer label mask. Vector Mode High-precision boundary adjustments, polygon vertex editing, batch lasso deletion Polygon contour representation with vertex manipulation and Lasso Delete.

docs.title: Editing Techniques
docs.text:
1. Separating Merged Lumens:
  2. In Raster mode, switch to the Eraser tool with a small radius (10–15 px) and draw a dividing cut through the shared wall.
  3. Run the connected component refresh to split into distinct labels.
  4. Removing False Detections & Clearing Resin Canals:
  5. Use the Lasso Selection tool in Vector mode to encircle non-tracheid structures, poorly detected tracheids (e.g., due to tissue overlap) or resin ducts, then press Delete (or use the Lasso Delete option) to remove all enclosed objects simultaneously.
  6. Restoring Overlooked Tracheids:
  7. Use the Brush tool in Raster mode or draw a new polygon in Vector mode over faint or damaged cell walls.

Figure 7: Using lasso selection to batch-remove resin canal cells and preparation artifacts.

docs.title: Step 4: Tree-Ring Editing & Boundary Curation
docs.text:
Accurate ring boundaries are essential because all radial cell positions and annual time series metrics depend on them. Open Plugins > ROXAS AI > 6 - Edit rings.

Tip: You can save your edits directly from within this widget at any time. Regularly saving edits is a good routine to preserve your work throughout the editing session.

Figure 8: Ring layer editor interface with polyline modification tools.

docs.title: Best Practices for Ring Boundary Tracing
docs.text:
• Ring boundaries must extend completely across the tangential width of the analyzed sample track.
  • Boundaries should align precisely along the latewood-earlywood transition (the outer wall of the terminal latewood tracheid row).
  • Ring lines must not self-intersect or cross neighboring ring boundaries.

docs.title: Recommended Vertex Editing Strategies
docs.text:
Editing ring polylines in napari requires an efficient vertex manipulation strategy:

Vertex Deletion and Addition Sequence

When deleting existing vertices and immediately adding new vertices within the same uninterrupted editing action, polygon/polyline indexing can connect the new vertices in an unexpected sequence (such as creating self-intersecting loops or back-tracking lines).

Rule: Always confirm/apply your changes after deleting vertices before starting a new edit action to insert additional vertices.

docs.title: The Polyline Reset Strategy (Fastest Reconstruction)
docs.text:
When an automatically detected ring boundary has significant geometric deviations or artifacts, attempting to move individual vertices or perform mixed delete/insert operations often takes excessive time. Instead, use a reset strategy:

  1. Delete the defective ring boundary or clear its internal vertices.
  2. Draw a simple polyline with at least three points (beginning, intermediate, and end point across the lateral margins), as napari requires a minimum of three vertices before additional intermediate points can be inserted into the line.
  3. Switch to vertex addition/insertion mode: Starting from one margin and progressing systematically toward the other, insert intermediate vertices along the actual anatomical boundary. Only place as many vertices as necessary to capture curvature and local boundary transitions.

This approach ensures minimal vertex count, eliminates loop artifacts, and is substantially faster than cleaning up messy automated traces.

Figure 9: Polyline reset strategy: (A) draw initial polyline with minimum vertices; (B) sequentially insert critical intermediate vertices along the terminal latewood boundary.

docs.title: Handling Missing, Wedging, and False Rings
docs.text:
• Mis-detected Rings: If the deep-learning model identified a wrong ring boundary, delete the boundary line. The calendar years of subsequent rings will automatically update in sequence.
  • Wedging Rings: When two rings share part of their boundary, trace the boundary of the wedging ring up to the point of convergence, then finish off neatly. Alternatively, copy and paste the partly shared ring to create a separate ring. Then, adjust the vertices in the wedging portion to match the correct ring boundary. Therefore, you can either reposition the existing vertices individually or use the lasso delete option to remove misplaced vertices and add new ones along the correct boundary.
  • Missing Rings: Insert a new polyline at the expected anatomical position by copy-pasting the ring that should be duplicated. ROXAS AI will re-index all ring labels and calendar years accordingly.

docs.title: Step 5: Visual Cross-Dating & Ring Synchronization
docs.text:
To verify ring counts and calendar year assignments against its reference series or the mean chronology, open Plugins > ROXAS AI > 7 - Visual cross-dating.

Figure 10: Visual cross-dating plotter showing sample ring widths (red) synchronized against reference series (yellow) and mean chronology (white).

  1. Select Reference Series: Choose the active sample or master chronology from the series list.
  2. Inspect Ring-Width Plots: Examine the curve overlay in raw or log-transformed scale. Characteristic pointer years (exceptionally narrow or wide rings) provide anchor points.
  3. Adjust Dating:
  4. If a missing ring is detected, return to 6 - Edit rings, insert the missing boundary, and refresh the plot.
  5. If an offset exists, update the outermost year or shift the series interactively.
  6. Confirm Calibration: Once the growth patterns match reference marker years, the chronological alignment is validated.

docs.title: Step 6: Saving Verified Annotations
docs.text:
While you can save edits directly from Widgets 5 and 6 during editing sessions, you can also use Plugins > ROXAS AI > 8 - Save cells & rings editing to review and persist all modified layers simultaneously.

  1. Open Plugins > ROXAS AI > 8 - Save cells & rings editing.
  2. Select the active sample and confirm layer selections.
  3. Click Save Layers.
  4. The system updates the synchronized files on disk:
  5. <sample>.cells.png: 16-bit or 32-bit cell label mask.
  6. <sample>.rings.tif: Vectorized ring boundary masks and calibrated ring identifiers.
  7. <sample>.metadata.json: Updated metadata including user edits and verification timestamps.

Figure 11: Saving finalized annotation layers to disk.

docs.title: Step 7: Anatomical Traits Extraction & Chronology Export
docs.text:
1. Open Plugins > ROXAS AI > 9A - Measure cells & rings (individual image).
  2. (Optional) If you wish to review or adjust default measurement parameters (such as CWT calculation options or tangential sector bands), open the Settings widget directly from the button inside this widget.
  3. Click Run Measurements.

docs.title: Generated Output Tables
docs.text:
The measurement engine outputs two primary text tables in the sample directory (as .txt or .csv, depending on your settings):

  • <sample>.cells_table.txt / .csv: Individual cell-level records (e.g., cell ID CID, ring affiliation year YEAR, lumen area LA, radial/tangential/overall cell wall thickness CWTRAD/CWTTAN/CWTALL, relative radial position RRADDISTR, and Mork's index RTSR).
  • <sample>.rings_table.txt / .csv: Ring-level summary records (e.g., calendar year YEAR, mean ring width MRW, cell count CNO, mean lumen area MLA, cell density CD, and mean cell wall thickness CWTALL).

For the complete list of all measured anatomical variables, abbreviations, theoretical hydraulic traits, and unit definitions, see the Technical Reference: Output Variables.

Figure 12: Measurement summary and exported tabular time series.

docs.title: 3. Production Workflow: Batch Processing Multi-Sample Studies
docs.text:
When analyzing dozens or hundreds of wood sections, ROXAS AI allows automated batch processing to minimize hands-on computer time.

flowchart TD
    B1["Batch Preparation (Widget 1)"] --> B2["Batch Cell & Ring Segmentation (Widget 3B)"]
    B2 --> B3["Targeted Manual Editing (Widgets 2, 5, 6, 7, 8)"]
    B3 --> B4["Batch Trait Extraction (Widget 9B)"]

docs.title: Step 1: Batch Preparation & Standardization
docs.text:
1. Organize raw scans into your designated project folder.
  2. Launch Plugins > ROXAS AI > 1 - Prepare project images for analysis.
  3. Choose the directory and batch-assign spatial resolution and metadata across all matching images.

Figure 13: Batch image preparation and metadata assignment.

docs.title: Step 2: Batch Cell & Ring Segmentation
docs.text:
1. Open Plugins > ROXAS AI > 3B - Batch detect cells & rings.
  2. Select your project directory (or manually select specific sample files to include in the batch run) and choose desired segmentation models.
  3. Click Run Batch Segmentation.
  4. The background queue sequentially processes each image, generating .cells.png and .rings.tif masks without requiring manual interaction for each image.

Figure 14: Batch segmentation execution and progress tracking.

docs.title: Step 3: Targeted Quality Control
docs.text:
1. Open Plugins > ROXAS AI > 2/4 - Load image(s).
  2. Iterate through processed samples.
  3. Perform targeted manual editing using Widgets 5, 6, 7, and 8.

docs.title: Step 4: Automated Batch Measurement Extraction
docs.text:
1. Open Plugins > ROXAS AI > 9B - Batch measure cells & rings.
  2. Select the project directory or manually select the images to process, then choose the desired options for anatomical trait calculation.
  3. Click Measure & Update.
  4. Measurement tables (.cells_table.txt and .rings_table.txt) are generated for all samples across the entire project directory.

Figure 15: Batch measurement extraction over multiple sample directories.

docs.title: User Guide: Widgets & Tools
docs.text:
ROXAS AI provides a modular suite of widgets within the napari environment designed to take your wood cross-section images through the entire Quantitative Wood Anatomy (QWA) pipeline—from raw anatomical image to deep-learning segmentation, interactive manual curation, visual cross-dating, and measurement of anatomical traits.

Widgets are numbered in the napari Plugins > ROXAS AI menu according to their typical execution sequence.

docs.title: Overview of the Workflow & Widgets
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["0 - Define Project Directory"] --> B["1 - Prepare Project Images"]
    B --> C["2/4 - Load Image(s)"]
    C --> D["3A - Detect Cells & Rings / 3B - Batch Detect"]
    D --> E["5 - Edit Cells"]
    D --> F["6 - Edit Rings"]
    F --> G["7 - Visual Cross-Dating"]
    E --> H["8 - Save Editing"]
